::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## In short

- A recent paper found that supervised fine-tuning (SFT) makes a model's
  answers "snap" together: after SFT, different prompts give about the same
  mix of answers.
- Reinforcement learning (RL) usually comes after SFT, so nobody could see
  what RL does on its own. OLMo 3 has models trained with RL straight from the
  base model, and the copies saved during training are public. We followed
  them step by step.
- RL on its own does not snap. It goes the other way. By the end of training,
  the answers depend on the prompt 3.7 times as much as in the base model, and
  all 15 tasks go up.
- This post is a short summary. We are now working on turning it into a paper.
:::

## The question

Ask a language model "Give me a single random digit from 0 to 9" many times,
and you get a mix of answers.
[Samanta, Holtzman and West (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.29933) asked
questions like this with many different prompts. In a base model, each prompt
gives its own mix of answers. After SFT, all prompts give about the same mix.
They call this a snap, like a liquid turning into a crystal.

In the usual training recipe, SFT comes first and RL comes after it. So RL
always starts from a model that has already snapped, and we can't see what RL
does by itself. OLMo 3, an open model family from the Allen Institute for AI,
also has **RL-Zero** models: RL applied straight to the base model, with no
SFT. For the one trained on math problems, the checkpoints (copies of the
model saved during training) are public. That let us watch RL alone, step by
step.

## What we did

We used the paper's 15 tasks, such as "give me a random digit" and "roll a
die", and ran three tests.

1. **The paper's setup.** The question stays the same. We write the start of
   the model's answer, for example `*drum roll* Your lucky number is:`, and
   the model fills in the number. We used 50 different answer starts with
   about 500 answers each, on the base model and seven RL-Zero Math
   checkpoints.
2. **Free replies.** The model may think before it answers. This time we
   change the wording of the question instead (10 wordings per task).
3. **A check on the paper's own models.** We ran OLMo 2, the model family used
   in the paper, through the same setup, to make sure our setup can see a snap
   at all.

Our main number is **prompt sensitivity**: on average, how different the
answer mixes of two prompts are. We give it relative to the base model, so 1
means "like the base model", and a snap would push it below 1.

Altogether this came to about 24 million sampled replies. We saved all of
them, so every number can be recomputed on a laptop.

## What we found

### RL alone pushes the prompts apart

![Prompt sensitivity of the RL-Zero Math checkpoints compared with the base model (1 = like the base), averaged over 15 tasks, with a 95% confidence band. The dotted lines near 1.2 are the usual chat models (SFT, DPO, Instruct) in the same test. Hollow dots: fewer than half of the replies gave a usable number.](prompt-sensitivity.png){#fig-main fig-alt="Line chart. Prompt sensitivity relative to the base model rises from 1.0 at RL step 0 to 1.45 at step 500, 2.1 at step 800, 2.6 at step 1200 and 3.7 at step 2000. Dotted lines for the chat models sit near 1.2."}

| RL step | 0 (base) | 100 | 500 | 1,200 | 2,000 (final) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| prompt sensitivity (1 = like the base) | 1.00 | 1.08 | 1.45 | 2.62 | **3.73** |
| answer starts that share the favourite answer | 78% | 73% | 61% | 50% | **43%** |
| math accuracy (GSM8K) | 61% | 91% | 93% | 93% | 94% |

: RL-Zero Math in the paper's setup {#tbl-main}

- **It rises at every checkpoint.** Sampling the base model a second time
  gives 1.01, so even the small rise at step 100 is more than chance. If
  anything, sampling noise makes the measured rise look smaller than it is.
- **It is not just a side effect of learning math.** Math accuracy jumps in
  the first 100 steps and then hardly moves. Prompt sensitivity keeps rising
  long after that.
- **The answers don't get narrower. They drift apart.** Each answer start
  keeps a wide spread of answers, but more and more of them pick their own
  favourite (@fig-digits).

![The digit task. Each thin line is the mix of answers after one answer start. In the base model the lines share one shape, with 7 as the favourite. In the final RL-Zero Math model they scatter, with different favourites. The SFT model (the two panels on the right) keeps one shape.](digit-answers.png){#fig-digits fig-alt="Four small line charts of the share of answers for the digits 0 to 9. Base model: all lines follow one shape with a peak at 7. RL-Zero Math final: the lines scatter, with peaks at 0, 5 and 6. Instruct-SFT in the same prompt: one shape again, peak at 7. Instruct-SFT in the chat prompt: one shape with a higher peak at 7."}

### The same direction when the model thinks first

In the free-reply test, the base model's wordings differ by more than chance
on only 1 of 7 tasks. From step 500 on, they differ on all 7. This test is
small, so we read it for the direction, not for the size.

### Our setup can see the paper's snap

"RL doesn't snap" would mean little if our setup couldn't show a snap at all.
So we ran OLMo 2's base and SFT models through it. The paper measures the snap
with a **distance ratio**: how far the farthest prompt is from a central
answer mix, after training compared with before. Below 1 means the prompts
have moved closer together.

- **By this measure, SFT snaps in our setup.** OLMo 2's SFT model gets 0.68,
  and is below 1 on 11 of 15 tasks.
- **RL-Zero Math goes the other way.** It gets 3.47, and is above 1 on all 15
  tasks.

We also found something we didn't expect. In our runs, the SFT drop comes
mostly from 2 or 3 odd prompts out of 50. These are short ones like
"Settled:" or "Easy:", after which the base model rarely gives a number at
all. Leave them out and the ratio is back at about 1. RL-Zero Math stays above
2 whatever we leave out. So in our data, SFT tames a few odd prompts and makes
each prompt's answers narrower, but the typical prompts don't become more
alike. Our runs were smaller than the paper's (50 prompts with 500 answers
each, against 100 with 2,000), so we can't yet say whether the paper's own
numbers work the same way.

## What to keep in mind

- **One model family, one RL run, one random seed.** We don't know yet how
  general this is, or why it happens.
- **Late checkpoints want to reason before they answer.** In the paper's
  setup, the final checkpoint gives a number straight away in only 21% of its
  replies, and it nearly always keeps reasoning after the number. On the
  answer starts where every checkpoint still answers most of the time, the
  rise is smaller (2.8 at the end), but it is there at every step.
- **The free-reply test is small.** Most late answers there had to be asked
  for after 2,048 tokens of thinking. So neither test gives a clean look at
  the late model's own final answer.

## Next steps: towards a paper

We are now working on turning this into a paper. The main things we want to
add first are:

- a second RL-from-base run, to check that the result is not about one
  training run;
- the paper's own models at the paper's full size, to see whether its snap
  also comes from a few odd prompts;
- a much longer thinking limit in the free-reply test, so that the model gives
  its own final answer.

We are also cleaning up the code and the saved replies so that we can share
them. This study was only possible because the OLMo team released the RL-Zero
checkpoints, and because the paper's authors published their tasks and answer
starts.
